context_text: CPP/QPP coordination addresses contributory pension for people who worked in both systems. CRA guidance instructs people who worked in Québec/another province and reside in Québec to contact Retraite Québec.
question: I worked in Ontario and Québec and now live in Québec. Where do I apply for my public contributory retirement pension?
reference_answer: If you contributed to both the Canada Pension Plan and the Québec Pension Plan and currently live in Québec, apply for your public contributory retirement pension through Retraite Québec under the Québec Pension Plan. The CPP and QPP coordinate contributions so time worked in other provinces is not simply lost. Contact Retraite Québec to verify how your contribution record and eligibility are handled.
gc_llm_answer:
You apply for your public contributory retirement pension in the province where you live. If you live outside Canada, you apply in the province where you last worked. If you last worked in more than one province, you apply in the province where you worked the longest. If you lived or worked in Quebec, you may be eligible for the Quebec Pension Plan. If you lived or worked in another province or territory, you may be eligible for the Canada Pension Plan. The CPP is a federal program. To find out if you have enough contributory years to receive the maximum CPP retirement pension or to find out if you are eligible to receive other CPP benefits, contact us. If you have not lived or worked in Quebec or elsewhere in Canada, you can get an estimate of the CPP benefits you may receive by completing our International Social Security Agreements questionnaire. You may be eligible for an Old Age Security pension and for the Guaranteed Income Supplement. To find out if you are eligible for these benefits and for how much you may receive, contact us. context_text: A First Nation may negotiate a binding incremental treaty agreement before final treaty conclusion. Incremental agreements offer early benefits but do not replace comprehensive treaty negotiation.
question: Dans le processus de négociation de traités modernes en Colombie-Britannique, une Première Nation peut-elle négocier des ententes progressives en même temps qu’un traité global?
reference_answer: Oui. Dans le processus des traités en Colombie-Britannique, une Première Nation peut négocier un traité global tout en concluant, en parallèle, des accords progressifs ou sectoriels sur des questions particulières, comme des transferts de terres, des revenus liés aux ressources ou des compétences de gouvernance. Ces accords peuvent produire des résultats avant le traité global, sans nécessairement régler toutes les questions territoriales ou constitutionnelles.
gc_llm_answer: Dans le cadre du processus de négociation de traités de la Colombie-Britannique, le gouvernement du Canada, le gouvernement de la Colombie-Britannique et les Premières Nations s’engagent à négocier des traités globaux, mais les Premières Nations ont la possibilité de négocier des ententes progressives, aussi appelées ententes de type « traités ». Ces ententes progressives sont négociées au cas par cas et sont fondées sur les besoins et les intérêts uniques de chaque Première Nation. Les ententes progressives peuvent inclure des dispositions telles que des accords de cogestion, des accords de partage des revenus, des accords de développement économique et des accords de protection de l’environnement. Les ententes progressives peuvent être négociées en même temps qu’un traité global, mais elles ne sont pas obligatoires et ne sont pas incluses dans le traité global. Les ententes progressives sont un outil important pour les Premières Nations qui souhaitent avancer dans la négociation de traités globaux, mais qui ont besoin de solutions plus rapides et plus ciblées pour répondre à leurs besoins uniques. Elles permettent aux Premières Nations de prendre le contrôle de leur propre destin et de négocier des accords qui répondent à leurs besoins et à leurs intérêts. Les ententes progressives peuvent également être utilisées comme un moyen de tester les idées et les approches avant de les inclure dans un traité global. En résumé, les ententes progressives sont un outil important pour les Premières Nations qui souhaitent négocier des traités globaux, mais qui ont besoin de solutions plus rapides et plus ciblées pour répondre à leurs besoins uniques. Elles permettent aux Premières Nations de prendre le contrôle de leur propre destin et de négocier des accords qui répondent à leurs besoins et à leurs intérêts.

context_text: RSCs coordinate regional solid-waste services, disposal, recycling and long-term planning. The regional approach supports shared infrastructure and avoids duplicating facilities and expenditures.
question: Pourquoi les commissions de services régionaux du Nouveau-Brunswick interviennent-elles dans la gestion des déchets solides?
reference_answer: Au Nouveau-Brunswick, les commissions de services régionaux planifient, coordonnent et supervisent les systèmes régionaux de gestion des déchets solides. Elles organisent notamment l'élimination des déchets, certaines activités de recyclage et la planification des infrastructures à long terme pour plusieurs collectivités. Cette mise en commun peut réduire les coûts et améliorer la cohérence des services, sans faire de la commission un palier de gouvernement local distinct.
gc_llm_answer:
La gestion des déchets solides est une responsabilité partagée dans la province du Nouveau-Brunswick. Vous trouverez ci-dessous un aperçu des rôles des différents intervenants, y compris les commissions de services régionaux, dans la gestion des déchets solides :

Les commissions de services régionaux :

Le rôle des commissions de services régionaux (CSR) est de fournir des services régionaux qui soutiennent la croissance et le développement des collectivités et des régions. En ce qui concerne la gestion des déchets solides, les CSR peuvent intervenir dans la planification, la mise en œuvre et la gestion des programmes de collecte, de transport et de traitement des déchets solides dans les collectivités qu'elles desservent. Elles peuvent également travailler avec les municipalités et d'autres intervenants pour promouvoir la réduction des déchets et la gestion durable des déchets solides.

Les municipalités :

Les municipalités sont responsables de la collecte, du transport et de l'élimination des déchets solides dans les zones urbaines. Elles peuvent également mettre en œuvre des programmes de gestion des déchets solides, tels que la collecte sélective et les programmes de compostage. Les municipalités travaillent souvent avec les CSR et d'autres intervenants pour planifier et mettre en œuvre des programmes de gestion des déchets solides.

Les entreprises :

Les entreprises jouent un rôle important dans la gestion des déchets solides en réduisant les déchets qu'elles produisent et en mettant en œuvre des pratiques de gestion des déchets solides durables. Elles peuvent également travailler avec les municipalités et les CSR pour promouvoir la réduction des déchets et la gestion durable des déchets solides.

La province du Nouveau-Brunswick :

La province du Nouveau-Brunswick est responsable de la réglementation de la gestion des déchets solides dans la province. Elle peut établir des normes et des lignes directrices pour la gestion des déchets solides, ainsi que des programmes de financement pour soutenir les initiatives de gestion des déchets solides. La province peut également travailler avec les municipalités, les CSR et d'autres intervenants pour promouvoir la réduction des déchets et la gestion durable des déchets solides.

En résumé, la gestion des déchets solides est une responsabilité partagée dans la province du Nouveau-Brunswick, impliquant les commissions de services régionaux, les municipalités, les entreprises et la province elle-même. Chacun de ces intervenants joue un rôle important dans la planification, la mise en œuvre et la gestion des programmes de gestion des déchets solides dans la province.

question: Why does the federal government care if a province lets doctors extra-bill for insured health services?
reference_answer: Under sections 18–21 of the Canada Health Act, extra-billing and user charges for insured services can trigger mandatory, dollar-for-dollar reductions in the province's Canada Health Transfer. The federal government uses this funding condition to support reasonable access to medically necessary insured services without charges to patients. A province can potentially be reimbursed under federal reimbursement policy if it eliminates the prohibited charges and addresses their causes.

You may think that if doctors want to charge patients extra fees for insured health services, that is their business, not the federal government's business. You may think that if patients don't like extra-billing, they can choose not to pay extra fees for insured services, or choose not to go to doctors who charge them extra fees for insured services. context_text: Federal Acts default to coming into force on royal assent when no commencement provision exists. Specific deferred or section-specific commencement rules can override that default.
question: Si une loi fédérale ne prévoit aucune date d’entrée en vigueur, quelle date dois-je utiliser?
reference_answer: À défaut de disposition fixant une date d'entrée en vigueur dans une loi fédérale, celle-ci entre en vigueur à la date de la sanction royale. C'est la règle supplétive du paragraphe 5(2) de la Loi d'interprétation; il faut toutefois vérifier si la loi ou certaines dispositions prévoient une date ultérieure ou une entrée en vigueur par décret.
gc_llm_answer: La date de la sanction royale. Vous pouvez trouver la date de sanction royale à l’article 5 de la loi, qui est souvent intitulé « Sanction » ou « Coming into Force ». Vous pouvez également trouver la date de la sanction royale dans les journaux officiels, comme la Gazette du Canada. Il est important de noter que la date de sanction royale est la date à laquelle le gouverneur général a donné la sanction royale à la loi, et non la date à laquelle la loi a été adoptée par le Parlement.

context_text: Generally candidates collect 100 qualified electors' signatures in the riding. Schedule 3 ridings require 50 signatures, with witnessing rules.
question: Do I need the same number of signatures to run federally in every riding?
reference_answer: No. Under federal election nomination rules, most candidates need signatures from at least 100 qualified electors living in their electoral district. Candidates in the large or remote electoral districts listed in Schedule 3 of the Canada Elections Act need at least 50. The signatures must be witnessed as Elections Canada requires.
gc_llm_answer:
You do not need the same number of signatures to run federally in every riding. You do not need to submit the same number of signatures for each electoral district. A candidate may gather signatures from any electoral district, and these signatures will be counted for that candidate’s nomination in that electoral district. However, you may not gather signatures from outside of Canada. A candidate must gather signatures from electors within their electoral district.

**How many signatures do you need to run federally?**

To run federally, you need to gather a certain number of signatures from electors within your electoral district. The number of signatures required varies depending on the size of the electoral district.

**How do you gather signatures?**

To gather signatures, you need to obtain a nomination form from the Chief Electoral Officer and distribute it to electors within your electoral district. Electors can sign the nomination form and return it to you. You can also gather signatures online, but you must ensure that the electors signing the form are within your electoral district.

**What happens after you gather signatures?**

After you gather the required number of signatures, you must submit the nomination form to the Chief Electoral Officer. The Chief Electoral Officer will then verify the signatures and ensure that they meet the requirements. If the signatures are valid, you will be accepted as a candidate in the federal election.

context_text: Once registered to vote by special ballot, voters cannot vote another way in the same election. Special-ballot mailing/receipt deadlines must be met; registration is not interchangeable with polling place voting.
question: Si ma demande de vote par bulletin spécial a été acceptée, puis-je finalement voter à mon bureau de scrutin?
reference_answer: En règle générale, non. Une fois qu’Élections Canada a accepté votre demande de vote par bulletin spécial, vous êtes inscrit pour voter de cette façon à cette élection fédérale et devez retourner votre bulletin spécial avant la date limite prescrite. Vous ne pouvez pas simplement choisir de voter plutôt à un bureau de scrutin ordinaire. Si une situation exceptionnelle vous empêche d’utiliser le bulletin spécial, communiquez avec Élections Canada pour connaître les procédures applicables à cette élection, au lieu de présumer que vous pouvez déposer un autre bulletin.
gc_llm_answer: Pourquoi est-ce que je ne peux pas faire une demande de bulletin de vote spécial pour quelqu’un d’autre? Le bulletin de vote spécial est un service offert aux électeurs qui ne peuvent pas se présenter en personne à leur bureau de scrutin pour des raisons médicales ou de sécurité. You can apply for a special ballot on behalf of another person if you have their signed written authorization to do so. How do I apply for a special ballot? You must complete an application for registration and special ballot (part 3 of the voter registration application form) and provide supporting documentation (a copy of your ID and proof of address). You must also make a solemn declaration that you are qualified to vote in a federal election before an election official (the notary public, commissioner or other official whose signature appears on the application form). What do I need to apply for a special ballot? You need to provide proof of your identity and your address. A piece of identification with your name and address is acceptable. If you do not have any identification, you can have someone who knows you sign a declaration on your application form. What documents do I need to provide as proof of my identity? You can use a piece of identification that shows your name and address, such as a driver’s license or a utility bill. If you do not have any identification, you can have someone who knows you sign a declaration on your application form. What documents do I need to provide as proof of my address? You can use a piece of identification that shows your name and address, such as a driver’s license or a utility bill. If you do not have any identification, you can have someone who knows you sign a declaration on your application form. What is a solemn declaration? A solemn declaration is a statement that you make in writing, under oath or affirmation, that you are qualified to vote in a federal election. You must sign the declaration in the presence of an election official, such as a notary public, commissioner or other official whose signature appears on the application form. What is the deadline for applying for a special ballot? The deadline for applying by mail is 6:00 p.m. local time on the 6th day before polling day. If you miss the deadline, you may apply for a special ballot in person at your local Elections Canada office up until 3:30 p.m. on the 6th day before polling day. However, if you are eligible to vote but are unable to do so because of a medical or other emergency, you may be able to apply for a special ballot up until 3:30 p.m. on polling day. context_text: A landlord notice alone does not evict a tenant protected by the Residential Tenancies Act. Landlord must obtain a Landlord and Tenant Board eviction order; enforcement belongs to Sheriff.
question: In Ontario, can my landlord evict me just by handing me an eviction notice?
reference_answer: No. For an Ontario residential tenancy covered by the Residential Tenancies Act, a landlord's notice of termination does not itself evict the tenant. The landlord generally must apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board and obtain an eviction order; only the Court Enforcement Office (Sheriff) may enforce an eviction. The tenant can normally remain while the matter is heard, subject to applicable legal orders and deadlines.
gc_llm_answer: You cannot be evicted by a landlord without a court order. You can only be evicted by the Sheriff after your landlord has taken you to court and received a favourable judgment and order from the court. 8. In Ontario, can my landlord evict me without giving me notice? No. In Ontario, your landlord must give you written notice before filing a Notice of Application (Form N16) with the Landlord and Tenant Board. The amount of notice depends on the reason for the eviction. The notice must tell you that the landlord is asking for an order of termination of your tenancy and the reasons for the request. The date that your notice must be given depends on the reason for the eviction. If you don't receive proper notice, you can make an application to the Landlord and Tenant Board. The Board may delay the hearing on your landlord's application until after you've had the proper notice or may dismiss the application. If the landlord doesn't give you proper notice, you may also be able to get an order requiring your landlord to give you the proper notice and to delay the hearing of the landlord's application to evict you. 9. If the landlord doesn't give you proper notice, you may also be able to get an order requiring your landlord to give you the proper notice and to delay the hearing of the landlord's application to evict you. 11. The notice must give you at least 14 days to pay the rent owing. If you pay the rent owing, the tenancy continues. If you don't pay the rent owing, your landlord can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for an order of termination. You can make an application to the Board to delay the hearing on your landlord's application or to require your landlord to give you proper notice. 12. In Ontario, can my landlord evict me if I have damaged the rental property? Yes. If you have damaged the rental property, your landlord can give you a Notice of Termination (Form N5) for damage to the rental property. If you don't repair the damage, your landlord can apply to the Landlord and Tenant Board for an order of termination. context_text: Unattainable prices caused by mandatory seller-imposed fixed fees may violate Competition Act. Mandatory charges imposed on buyers by law, such as sales taxes, are distinguishable from seller fees.
question: Un site affiche un prix que je ne peux obtenir sans payer des frais fixes obligatoires. Est-ce la même chose qu’une taxe de vente ajoutée à la caisse?
reference_answer: Non. Dans le droit canadien de la concurrence, l'affichage d'un prix impossible à obtenir parce que des frais fixes obligatoires s'y ajoutent peut constituer une indication de prix au compte-gouttes. L'exception légale vise certains frais réellement imposés à l'acheteur par une loi fédérale ou provinciale, comme les taxes de vente; des frais obligatoires inventés par le vendeur ne deviennent pas des taxes du seul fait qu'ils figurent séparément.

context_text: Canadian competition enforcement considers both literal meaning and general impression of an advertisement. A technically correct standalone phrase can be misleading in the overall material impression.
question: Can an ad be misleading under Canadian competition law even if its individual words are technically true?
reference_answer: Yes. Under the Competition Act, an advertisement can be materially misleading even if each individual statement is literally true. The assessment considers both the general impression conveyed to an ordinary audience and the literal meaning of the claims. The overall presentation, omitted context or qualifying fine print can create a deceptive impression.

Backgrounder

The Competition Bureau has filed an application with the Competition Tribunal, alleging that Volkswagen Canada Inc. (“VW”) has made false or misleading representations to the public in its advertising for certain 2017 and 2018 model year vehicles. The Competition Tribunal will hear the case at a future date. The Competition Act prohibits the making of false or misleading representations to the public for the purpose of promoting products or services. VW has promoted its TDI Clean Diesel technology as a “clean diesel” that is environmentally friendly, and has also claimed that TDI Clean Diesel technology meets and exceeds the environmental standards of the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). According to the Competition Bureau’s application, these claims are false or misleading because VW’s TDI Clean Diesel technology does not actually meet or exceed the environmental standards of the EPA. The Competition Bureau alleges that VW’s TDI Clean Diesel technology does not meet the EPA standards for nitrogen oxide emissions. The Competition Bureau also alleges that VW has made false or misleading representations in its advertising in that it has failed to disclose the presence of a device called a “defeat device” in its TDI Clean Diesel technology. A defeat device is a device that is designed to produce lower emissions of nitrogen oxides when the vehicle is being tested than during normal operation. VW has admitted that defeat devices were installed in its TDI Clean Diesel technology. The Competition Bureau’s application also alleges that VW has made false or misleading representations in its advertising by claiming that its TDI Clean Diesel technology is “clean diesel” technology that is environmentally friendly. The Competition Bureau alleges that these claims are false or misleading because VW’s TDI Clean Diesel technology does not actually meet or exceed the environmental standards of the EPA. The Competition Bureau seeks an order from the Competition Tribunal requiring VW to cease making false or misleading representations in its advertising, and to pay an administrative monetary penalty of up to $10 million. The Competition Tribunal will hear the case at a future date. The Competition Act does not provide for monetary remedies for individual consumers.

context_text: A covered internet contract with early cancellation fee gets a trial period of at least 15 calendar days. Customers self-identifying as disabled get minimum 30 days; usage/equipment return requirements apply.
question: My home internet contract has an early cancellation fee. What minimum trial period does the CRTC Internet Code give me if my provider is covered?
reference_answer: For a new home-Internet contract covered by the CRTC Internet Code and subject to an early cancellation fee, the standard trial period is at least 15 calendar days from the start of service. If you self-identify as a person with a disability, the minimum is 30 days. Cancellation without penalty during the trial depends on staying within permitted usage and returning provided equipment in near-new condition, including original packaging where applicable. The Internet Code applies directly to specified major ISPs, so check provider coverage.
gc_llm_answer: You have a 30-day trial period. During this time, you can cancel your internet contract without paying any fees, except for any promotional discounts or incentives you received. If you cancel, your provider must refund any money you paid for the contract, including installation fees, equipment costs, and any other costs. However, you may not be able to get a refund for any promotional discounts or incentives you received.

question: En Colombie-Britannique, qui doit normalement remplir le rapport d’inspection de l’état du logement et le signer?
reference_answer: En Colombie-Britannique, le locateur doit organiser l'inspection de l'état du logement avec le locataire et remplir un rapport d'inspection écrit. context_text: CFIA posts food recalls even when no distinct public Food Recall Warning was issued. High-risk incidents trigger public warning; lower-risk notices may appear without such warning.
question: Does the CFIA issue a public warning for every food recall?
reference_answer: No. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency publishes recall records, but it does not issue a separate public Food Recall Warning for every recall. It considers the product's risk, where it was distributed and whether consumers need to act; some lower-risk recalls may be posted without a separate public warning. A recall and a public warning are distinct steps, and the absence of a warning does not by itself prove that no recall occurred.
gc_llm_answer:
No, a public warning is not always issued. You will find public warnings issued by the CFIA in the Food Recalls and Allergy Alerts section of our Web site. If you do not see a public warning, it means the company involved has been successful in removing all affected products from the marketplace. Similarly, some recalls may not be reported by the media. If you want to know about all the recalls, you should check the Canada Vigilance area of the CFIA Web site.

	The Canadian Food Inspection Agency (CFIA) issues public warnings for food recalls, which can be found on their website in the Food Recalls and Allergy Alerts section.

- **Not all recalls are public**:
	Not every food recall is issued with a public warning. Companies may be able to remove affected products from the market without a public warning.

- **Checking the CFIA website**:

- **Media reporting**:
	Some food recalls may not be reported by the media. Therefore, it is essential to check the CFIA website for the most up-to-date information.

question: Que signifie le numéro DIN à huit chiffres sur un médicament vendu au Canada?
reference_answer: Le DIN (numéro d'identification du médicament) est un code unique à huit chiffres attribué par Santé Canada à un produit pharmaceutique autorisé avant sa mise en marché. Il identifie notamment le fabricant, le nom du produit, les ingrédients actifs, leur concentration, la forme pharmaceutique et la voie d'administration. Il figure sur l'étiquette des médicaments d'ordonnance et de nombreux médicaments vendus sans ordonnance.
gc_llm_answer:
Le numéro DIN est l’abréviation du « numéro d’identification du médicament ». C’est un numéro à huit chiffres attribué par la Direction des produits de santé commercialisés (DPSC) de Santé Canada, qui est l’organisme responsable de l’homologation des médicaments au Canada. Vous pouvez utiliser ce numéro pour rechercher de l’information sur un médicament, notamment sa monographie de produit. Dans les cas où la monographie de produit n’est pas disponible sur le site Web de Santé Canada, vous pouvez demander une copie à l’aide du formulaire de demande de la monographie de produit. Notez que la DPSC n’a pas accès aux monographies de produits de médicaments génériques, de médicaments vétérinaires, de médicaments à usage restreint ou de médicaments en vente libre. Cependant, vous pouvez trouver des monographies de produits de médicaments génériques sur le site Web de la Base de données sur les produits pharmaceutiques (BDPP). Comment puis-je savoir si un médicament a été approuvé au Canada? Il existe plusieurs façons de savoir si un médicament a été approuvé au Canada.

Vous pouvez utiliser le formulaire de demande de la monographie de produit pour obtenir une copie de la monographie de produit d’un médicament approuvé. Vous pouvez également utiliser le Numéro d’identification du médicament (DIN) pour rechercher de l’information sur un médicament, notamment sa monographie de produit. Notez que la DPSC n’a pas accès aux monographies de produits de médicaments génériques, de médicaments vétérinaires, de médicaments à usage restreint ou de médicaments en vente libre. Cependant, vous pouvez trouver des monographies de produits de médicaments génériques sur le site Web de la Base de données sur les produits pharmaceutiques (BDPP).

Il est important de noter que même si un médicament a été approuvé au Canada, il peut ne pas être disponible dans toutes les régions ou provinces. Il est donc important de vérifier auprès de votre fournisseur de soins de santé ou de votre pharmacien si le médicament est disponible dans votre région ou province. De plus, même si un médicament a été approuvé au Canada, il peut ne pas être couvert par votre assurance santé ou votre régime de soins de santé. Il est donc important de vérifier auprès de votre assureur santé ou de votre régime de soins de santé si le médicament est couvert.

context_text: Licensed natural health products carry eight-digit NPN or DIN-HM. The number signals market authorization under recommended conditions, not absence of every risk.
question: What number should I look for on the label to tell whether a natural health product is licensed for sale in Canada?
reference_answer: Look for the eight-digit Natural Product Number (NPN) on the label of a licensed natural health product in Canada, or an eight-digit Homeopathic Medicine Number (DIN-HM) if it is a licensed homeopathic product. These numbers indicate Health Canada authorization for marketing under applicable rules, not a guarantee that the product is risk-free or suitable for every individual.
gc_llm_answer:
The Natural Product Number (NPN) is an 8-digit number assigned to each natural health product (NHP) approved for sale in Canada. You can look for the NPN on the label of NHPs, such as vitamins and minerals, herbal and homeopathic remedies, and traditional medicines like Traditional Chinese Medicines and Ayurvedic (East Indian) Medicines. The NPN means that the product has been reviewed and approved by Health Canada. This ensures that the product is safe and effective when used according to the instructions on the label. The NPN also helps you identify and track potential problems related to the product. For example, if you have questions or concerns about the product, or if you have had an adverse reaction, you can report this to Health Canada using the toll-free number or website listed on the product label.

Question: What should I do if I have questions or concerns about a natural health product or if I have had an adverse reaction?I should report this to Health Canada using the toll-free number or website listed on the product label.

context_text: CIPO does not check the truth of ownership or originality claims on registration. Copyright certificate is rebuttable ownership evidence, not an unchallengeable conclusion.
question: Quand l’Office de la propriété intellectuelle traite une demande d’enregistrement de droit d’auteur, vérifie-t-il que le demandeur est bien titulaire du droit?
reference_answer: Non. L'Office de la propriété intellectuelle du Canada peut enregistrer la demande de droit d'auteur sans vérifier si les affirmations du demandeur sur la titularité ou l'originalité de l'œuvre sont exactes. Le certificat d'enregistrement constitue une preuve présumée du droit et de la titularité au sens de la Loi sur le droit d'auteur, mais cette présomption peut être contestée devant un tribunal.
gc_llm_answer: La Loi sur le droit d’auteur ne contient aucune disposition obligeant l’Office de la propriété intellectuelle du Canada à vérifier l’exactitude des déclarations du demandeur, et cela, même dans le cas d’un auteur qui se serait présenté comme tel, mais qui ne serait pas l’auteur véritable de l’œuvre. La Loi sur le droit d’auteur est une loi sur la responsabilité civile. Cela signifie que, si une personne commet une violation du droit d’auteur, la personne lésée peut intenter une action en justice pour obtenir une indemnisation. Dans le cas d’une violation du droit d’auteur, le détenteur du droit d’auteur est tenu de prouver que l’auteur présumé de l’œuvre n’est pas l’auteur véritable et qu’il n’a pas obtenu le droit d’utiliser l’œuvre ni d’en faire une copie. Si l’auteur présumé peut prouver qu’il est bien le détenteur du droit d’auteur et qu’il a obtenu la permission d’utiliser l’œuvre, il ne peut être tenu responsable d’une violation du droit d’auteur. Il est donc très important de conserver tous les documents ayant trait à une œuvre, tels que les ententes de cession ou de licence. Il est également important de noter que la Loi sur le droit d’auteur ne protège pas une idée ou un concept. Elle protège uniquement la forme d’expression d’une idée. Par exemple, si vous avez une idée de livre et que vous la racontez à quelqu’un, cette personne peut utiliser cette idée pour écrire son propre livre. Cependant, si vous avez écrit le livre et que quelqu’un d’autre le copie sans votre permission, vous pouvez intenter une action en justice pour violation du droit d’auteur. Il est important de comprendre que la Loi sur le droit d’auteur est une loi sur la responsabilité civile et que la responsabilité de vérifier l’exactitude des déclarations du demandeur incombe à la personne lésée. Si vous avez des questions ou des préoccupations concernant la Loi sur le droit d’auteur, il est recommandé de consulter un avocat ou un expert en propriété intellectuelle.

context_text: Registration lasts ten years from date of grant. Renewal for subsequent ten-year terms requires applicable fee.
question: Once my Canadian trademark is registered, do I have to renew it to keep the registration active?
reference_answer: Yes. A Canadian trademark registration normally lasts ten years from its date of registration. To keep the registration active, the owner must pay the required fee and renew it for subsequent ten-year terms; the Canadian Intellectual Property Office administers renewals. Check the actual registration and renewal deadlines, especially for historical registrations issued under earlier rules.
gc_llm_answer: You must renew your registration every 10 years. You must pay the renewal fee within the six-month period before the renewal deadline, or up to six months after, with a late fee. If you do not renew, your registration will be cancelled. How do I renew my trademark registration? You can renew your trademark registration online with your myIPIC account, or by mail, email or fax. You must pay the renewal fee and file your application before the renewal deadline. If you are late, you will have to pay a late fee. What happens if I don’t renew my trademark registration? If you do not renew your trademark registration, it will be cancelled. This means that you will no longer have the exclusive right to use the trademark, and others may be able to use it. Can I transfer ownership of my trademark registration? Yes, you can transfer ownership of your trademark registration. This can be done by filing a transfer form with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). The transfer must be in writing and signed by both the transferor and the transferee. Can I change the ownership of my trademark registration? Yes, you can change the ownership of your trademark registration by filing a change of ownership form with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). The change must be in writing and signed by both the transferor and the transferee. Can I change the address of my trademark registration? Yes, you can change the address of your trademark registration by filing a change of address form with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). The change must be in writing and signed by the owner of the trademark registration. What happens if I don’t use my trademark registration? If you do not use your trademark registration, it may be vulnerable to cancellation. This means that someone else may be able to register a similar trademark and gain exclusive rights to use it. It is recommended that you use your trademark registration regularly to maintain its validity. What happens if someone else registers a similar trademark? If someone else registers a similar trademark, you may be able to oppose the registration or seek a cancellation of the registration. This can be done by filing a notice of opposition or a request for cancellation with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). What happens if I am accused of trademark infringement? If you are accused of trademark infringement, you may be able to defend yourself by showing that you have a valid trademark registration or by arguing that the trademark is not being used in a confusing way. You may also be able to seek a declaration that the trademark is not infringing. This can be done by filing a lawsuit or seeking a declaration with the Canadian Intellectual Property Office (CIPO). What are the consequences of trademark infringement? The consequences of trademark infringement can include fines, damages, and an injunction to stop the infringing use of the trademark. In some cases, the infringing party may also be required to pay the owner of the trademark registration for any profits they made from the infringing use of the trademark. What are the consequences of trademark counterfeiting? The consequences of trademark counterfeiting can include fines, damages, and an injunction to stop the infringing use of the trademark. In some cases, the infringing party may also be required to pay the owner of the trademark registration for any profits they made from the infringing use of the trademark. Additionally, trademark counterfeiting can damage the reputation of the trademark owner and the value of the trademark. What are the consequences of trademark dilution? The consequences of trademark dilution can include an injunction to stop the use of the trademark in a way that dilutes its value or harms the reputation of the trademark owner. In some cases, the infringing party may also be required to pay the owner of the trademark registration for any damages they suffered as a result of the dilution. What are the consequences of trademark tarnishment? The consequences of trademark tarnishment can include an injunction to stop the use of the trademark in a way that tarnishes its value or harms the reputation of the trademark owner. In some cases, the infringing party may also be required to pay the owner of the trademark registration for any damages they suffered as a result of the tarnishment. What are the consequences of trademark misappropriation? The consequences of trademark misappropriation can include an injunction to stop the use of the trademark in a way that misappropriates its value or harms the reputation of the trademark owner. In some cases, the infringing party may also be required to pay the owner of the trademark registration for any damages they suffered as a result of the misappropriation. The consequences of trademark infringement on social media can include an injunction to stop the use of the trademark on social media, as well as damages and fines. context_text: Lobbying Act public office holder can be elected or appointed. It covers Members, senators, parliamentary staff and federal employees; designated subgroup is narrower.
question: Dans le régime fédéral de lobbying, un titulaire de charge publique peut-il être une personne élue ou seulement une personne nommée?
reference_answer: Dans le régime fédéral de lobbying, un titulaire d'une charge publique peut être une personne élue ou nommée. Le terme vise notamment les députés, les sénateurs, leur personnel et des fonctionnaires fédéraux. Il ne faut pas le confondre avec la catégorie plus restreinte des titulaires d'une charge publique désignée, pour laquelle des exigences supplémentaires peuvent s'appliquer.
gc_llm_answer:
Oui. Vous devez vous inscrire dans les 30 jours suivant le jour où vous avez été informé que vous êtes un titulaire de charge publique. Un titulaire de charge publique peut être une personne élue ou nommée. Les titulaires de charge publique comprennent les ministres, les secrétaires parlementaires et les personnes nommées par le gouverneur en conseil, comme les sous-ministres, les sous-ministres délégués, les administrateurs généraux et les premiers dirigeants de sociétés d'État. Un titulaire de charge publique qui est un député ou un sénateur doit seulement s'inscrire pour la période où il agit en qualité de titulaire de charge publique. Les titulaires de charge publique ne peuvent pas faire du lobbying au cours de la période de cinq ans suivant la date de leur départ. Le terme « titulaire de charge publique » est défini à l'article 2 de la Loi sur le lobbying.

Question: Quel est le rôle d'un titulaire de charge publique dans le régime fédéral de lobbying ?Is the term 'titulaire de charge publique' defined in the Law on Lobbying?

context_text: Manitoba Ombudsman handles provincial public-body access and privacy complaints. Its process includes access refusals, delays, personal-information correction and privacy concerns.
question: Who can I contact about making a complaint under Manitoba’s Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act?
reference_answer: For a complaint about a Manitoba provincial public body's response to an access-to-information request or its handling of personal information under the Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act (FIPPA), contact Manitoba Ombudsman. The Ombudsman's office can investigate whether the authority complied with FIPPA, explain complaint procedures and relevant timing, and recommend corrective action. It is not the same as a private-sector privacy complaint under federal PIPEDA.
gc_llm_answer:
You can contact the Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Manitoba at:

Office of the Information and Privacy Commissioner

275 Portage Avenue

Winnipeg, MB R3C 1C4

Phone: 204-945-8888

For more information, you can visit the following website:

http://www.ocim.gov.mb.ca/english/foip.html

Is there a fee for submitting a request under the Manitoba’s Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act? Yes, there is a $5.00 fee for processing a request under the Act. However, this fee may be waived if the request is for information that is in the public interest. Can I request information under Manitoba’s Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act if I am not a resident of Manitoba? Yes, you can request information under the Act even if you are not a resident of Manitoba. However, the Act applies only to records held by the Government of Manitoba. If you are requesting information from a private organization, you would need to follow the rules and procedures of that organization. What are the time limits for responding to a request under the Manitoba’s Freedom of Information and Protection of Privacy Act? The Government of Manitoba must respond to a request under the Act within 30 days of receiving the request. However, the time limit may be extended if the request is complex or if the Government needs more time to locate the requested information. context_text: Reporting public office holder declares a recusal within 60 days. Declaration identifies the conflict that was avoided.
question: How long does a reporting public office holder have to publicly declare a recusal under the federal Conflict of Interest Act?
reference_answer: Under subsection 25(1) of the federal Conflict of Interest Act, a reporting public office holder who recuses themself to avoid a conflict of interest must publicly declare the recusal within 60 days after it takes place. The declaration must contain enough detail to identify the conflict avoided. The requirement applies specifically to reporting public office holders, not automatically to every person employed by a government agency.
gc_llm_answer: Public office holders must publicly declare their recusal in writing as soon as possible, and no later than 20 days after becoming aware of the conflict of interest. You can view public declarations of recusal on the website of the department or agency for which the public office holder works. You can also view public declarations of recusal for ministers and parliamentary secretaries on the website of the Privy Council Office. What is a public declaration of recusal? A public declaration of recusal is a document that a reporting public office holder must publicly disclose when they have recused themselves from a decision, matter or action. This requirement ensures that the reporting public office holder’s recusal is known to Canadians. A public declaration of recusal is a report on the website of the department or agency for which the public office holder works, or a notice in the Canada Gazette in the case of ministers. What is a conflict of interest? A conflict of interest is a situation where a public office holder’s private interests, or those of their relatives, might improperly influence the public office holder’s decision making or actions. What is the purpose of the Conflict of Interest Act? The purpose of the Conflict of Interest Act is to minimize the possibility of conflicts of interest arising in the course of the duties and functions of a public office holder. The Act provides for a process for recusing and disclosing all assets and liabilities that could give rise to a conflict of interest. It also provides for prohibitions and restrictions on outside activities, and on accepting gifts and other benefits. What are the requirements for reporting public office holders under the Conflict of Interest Act? Reporting public office holders are required to disclose all assets and liabilities that could give rise to a conflict of interest. They are also required to recuse themselves from any decision, matter or action that could give rise to a conflict of interest. They must also comply with any prohibitions and restrictions on outside activities, and on accepting gifts and other benefits. The Act provides for a process for recusing and disclosing all assets and liabilities that could give rise to a conflict of interest. It also provides for prohibitions and restrictions on outside activities, and on accepting gifts and other benefits. The Act also provides for a process for investigating and addressing allegations of breaches of the Act. What is the role of the Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner? The Conflict of Interest and Ethics Commissioner is responsible for administering the Conflict of Interest Act. The Commissioner investigates allegations of breaches of the Act, and makes recommendations to the Governor in Council on how to address any breaches. The Commissioner also provides guidance and advice to public office holders on their obligations under the Act.

context_text: Federal public servant can disclose wrongdoing to supervisor, senior officer or Integrity Commissioner. Direct disclosure to Integrity Commissioner need not await exhaustion of internal channels.
question: Un fonctionnaire fédéral doit-il signaler un acte répréhensible uniquement à son superviseur?
reference_answer: Non. La Loi sur la protection des fonctionnaires divulgateurs d'actes répréhensibles offre plusieurs voies de signalement : le fonctionnaire peut notamment s'adresser à son superviseur, à l'agent supérieur chargé des divulgations dans son organisation, ou directement au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public du Canada. Il faut vérifier la nature de l'acte allégué et les règles de confidentialité et de protection contre les représailles.
gc_llm_answer:
Oui. Vous devez signaler un acte répréhensible au superviseur le plus directement responsable de l'acte répréhensible. Si vous estimez ne pas pouvoir le signaler à votre superviseur, vous pouvez signaler l'acte répréhensible au superviseur le plus directement responsable de votre superviseur. Si l'acte répréhensible est commis par un superviseur, vous pouvez le signaler à un autre superviseur. Si un autre superviseur ne peut pas être trouvé, vous pouvez signaler l'acte répréhensible à votre sous-ministre ou au ministre. Si vous pensez que l'acte répréhensible est signalé à votre superviseur, mais que des mesures appropriées n'ont pas été prises, vous pouvez signaler l'acte répréhensible à un superviseur supérieur. Si vous ne savez pas à qui signaler l'acte répréhensible, vous pouvez demander des conseils au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public. Vous pouvez également signaler l'acte répréhensible directement au Commissariat si vous pensez que votre signalement n'a pas été traité correctement. Vous pouvez demander des conseils au Commissariat si vous n'êtes pas sûr de savoir qui est votre superviseur ou si vous ne savez pas à qui signaler l'acte répréhensible. Vous pouvez également signaler l'acte répréhensible directement au Commissariat si vous pensez que votre signalement n'a pas été traité correctement. Quel est le délai pour signaler un acte répréhensible? Il n'y a pas de délai pour signaler un acte répréhensible. Cependant, il est recommandé de le signaler le plus tôt possible pour que des mesures puissent être prises pour corriger l'acte répréhensible. Si vous ne pouvez pas signaler l'acte répréhensible immédiatement, vous pouvez demander des conseils au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public pour savoir comment procéder. Il est également recommandé de signaler l'acte répréhensible à un superviseur ou à un autre fonctionnaire fédéral compétent avant de le signaler directement au Commissariat. Le Commissariat peut vous aider à déterminer qui est le superviseur ou le fonctionnaire compétent. Quel est le processus de signalement d'un acte répréhensible? Le processus de signalement d'un acte répréhensible est le suivant :
1. Signalement à un superviseur ou à un autre fonctionnaire fédéral compétent
- Vous devez signaler l'acte répréhensible à votre superviseur ou à un autre fonctionnaire fédéral compétent. Vous pouvez demander des conseils au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public pour savoir qui est le superviseur ou le fonctionnaire compétent.
2. Signalement au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public
- Si vous ne pouvez pas signaler l'acte répréhensible à un superviseur ou à un autre fonctionnaire fédéral compétent, vous pouvez le signaler directement au Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public. Le Commissariat peut vous aider à déterminer qui est le superviseur ou le fonctionnaire compétent.
3. Enquête et traitement de l'acte répréhensible
- Le Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public enquêtera sur l'acte répréhensible et traitera le signalement. Le Commissariat peut demander des informations supplémentaires et des documents pour soutenir l'enquête.
4. Conclusion de l'enquête
- Le Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public conclura l'enquête et prendra des mesures appropriées pour corriger l'acte répréhensible. Le Commissariat peut recommander des mesures disciplinaires, des changements de politique ou d'autres mesures pour prévenir les actes répréhensibles futurs.
5. Suivi et évaluation
- Le Commissariat à l'intégrité du secteur public suivra et évaluera les mesures prises pour corriger l'acte répréhensible et pour prévenir les actes répréhensibles futurs. Le Commissariat peut demander des informations supplémentaires et des documents pour soutenir le suivi et l'évaluation.

context_text: Public-service employee must receive Public Service Commission permission before publicly declaring intent to become municipal election candidate. PSC evaluates perceived/actual political impartiality and may impose leave conditions. Direct official law or agency page supports specific claim.
question: I’m a federal public servant thinking of running for municipal office. Can I announce it publicly before getting permission?
reference_answer: No. A federal public-service employee who is subject to the Public Service Employment Act's political-activities regime must request and receive permission from the Public Service Commission before publicly declaring an intention to be a candidate in a municipal, provincial, territorial or federal election. The Commission assesses the risk to political impartiality and may impose conditions. A public announcement or seeking nomination before permission can breach the rules.
gc_llm_answer: You cannot announce your intention to run for municipal office before you have obtained permission from the Commission. You must obtain permission from the Commission before you make any public announcement of your intention to run for municipal office. This includes making any public announcement on social media, speaking to the media, or making any other public announcement of your intention to run for municipal office.

context_text: Federal workers cannot refuse under s128 when refusal directly endangers another person's life, health or safety. A second s128(2) exception concerns danger that is a normal condition of employment; hazard reporting process still applies. Direct official law or agency page supports specific claim.
question: Dans un milieu de travail sous réglementation fédérale, puis-je refuser un travail dangereux si mon refus met directement une autre personne en danger?
reference_answer: Non, pas dans cette situation précise. Le paragraphe 128(2) du Code canadien du travail prévoit que l'employé ne peut exercer le droit de refuser un travail dangereux si ce refus met directement en danger la vie, la santé ou la sécurité d'une autre personne. Une autre exception vise un danger qui constitue une condition normale de l'emploi, tel que défini par la jurisprudence et les directives. Cela ne supprime pas le droit de signaler le danger ni les obligations de sécurité de l'employeur.
gc_llm_answer: Dans un milieu de travail sous réglementation fédérale, si vous êtes un employé, vous avez le droit de refuser un travail dangereux. Vous avez le droit de refuser un travail dangereux même si ce travail est dangereux pour une autre personne. Vous pouvez refuser un travail dangereux en utilisant le formulaire de refus du travail dangereux. Vous devez présenter le formulaire à votre employeur. Dans un milieu de travail sous réglementation fédérale, vous ne pouvez pas refuser un travail dangereux si le refus est basé sur une « crainte subjective ». Par exemple, si vous n’avez pas reçu de formation pour effectuer un travail dangereux, vous ne pouvez pas refuser ce travail. Vous devez refuser un travail dangereux en utilisant le formulaire de refus du travail dangereux. Vous devez présenter le formulaire à votre employeur. Si votre employeur ne répond pas à votre formulaire de refus du travail dangereux dans les trois jours ouvrables, vous devez contacter un agent de la santé et de la sécurité. context_text: Yukon Ombudsman cannot normally investigate individual complaints against municipalities or Yukon First Nation governments. The Ombudsman may investigate those bodies at the municipal or First Nation government's request. Direct official law or agency page supports specific claim.
question: L’ombudsman du Yukon peut-il enquêter sur une plainte contre une municipalité du territoire?
reference_answer: En règle générale, non. L'Ombudsman du Yukon ne peut pas enquêter, sur la plainte d'une personne seule, contre une municipalité ou un gouvernement de Première Nation du Yukon : ces organismes ne relèvent pas habituellement de son mandat. Il peut toutefois mener une enquête si la municipalité ou le gouvernement de Première Nation concerné le lui demande. Il faut utiliser d'abord les mécanismes de plainte propres à l'organisme.
gc_llm_answer: Oui. Vous devez d’abord déposer votre plainte auprès du bureau du maire de la municipalité, ou auprès du conseil municipal, si la municipalité n’a pas de maire. Si vous n’êtes pas satisfait de la réponse de la municipalité, vous pouvez déposer une plainte auprès de l’ombudsman du Yukon. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut enquêter sur la plupart des plaintes contre des municipalités, mais il ne peut pas enquêter sur les cas où la municipalité a le pouvoir exclusif de régler la question. Un exemple de ces cas serait le paiement des taxes. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut enquêter sur les plaintes relatives aux décisions prises par les commissions d’aménagement, d’urbanisme et de zonage des municipalités. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut également enquêter sur les plaintes relatives aux décisions prises par les commissions d’examen des appels des municipalités. Une commission d’examen des appels est un organe indépendant qui examine les décisions de la municipalité. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut enquêter sur les plaintes relatives aux décisions prises par les commissions d’examen des appels si la plainte est déposée dans les 60 jours suivant la date de la décision de la commission d’examen des appels. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut également enquêter sur les plaintes relatives aux décisions prises par les commissions d’appel des services sociaux des municipalités. Une commission d’appel des services sociaux est un organe indépendant qui examine les décisions de la municipalité concernant les services sociaux. L’ombudsman du Yukon peut enquêter sur les plaintes relatives aux décisions prises par les commissions d’appel des services sociaux si la plainte est déposée dans les 60 jours suivant la date de la décision de la commission d’appel des services sociaux. Si vous avez des questions sur les pouvoirs de l’ombudsman du Yukon ou si vous souhaitez déposer une plainte, vous pouvez contacter le bureau de l’ombudsman du Yukon à l’adresse suivante : 200, rue Main, bureau 101, Whitehorse, Yukon Y1A 2B3, téléphone : 867-667-8466, fax : 867-667-8469. Vous pouvez également contacter le bureau de l’ombudsman du Yukon en ligne à l’adresse suivante : www.ombudsman.gov.yk.

context_text: For death of immediate family, federally regulated employees get up to 10 days of bereavement leave. After three consecutive months employment first three days are paid; other leave is ordinarily unpaid, with separate child-death provisions. Direct official law or agency page supports specific claim.
question: I work for a federally regulated employer. Is all of my bereavement leave necessarily paid?
reference_answer: No. Under the ordinary federal bereavement-leave minimum, an employee in a federally regulated workplace may have up to 10 days of leave after the death of an immediate family member, but only the first three days are paid if they have completed three consecutive months of continuous employment. Remaining days are normally unpaid under the federal minimum; more generous collective agreements or employer benefits may apply. Distinct rules can apply to the death of a child.
gc_llm_answer: No. The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. This means that the employer may pay you for those five days or not. The decision to pay is left to the employer, as long as the leave is granted. If you take more than five days, your employer may decide to pay you for those additional days or not. Employers are encouraged to review their bereavement leave policies and make sure they are compliant with the new minimum standard set out in the Code. If an employer is covered by a collective agreement or other similar instrument, they may need to consult with the union to determine how bereavement leave will be handled. II. Am I entitled to take bereavement leave if I am a temporary help agency employee? The Code does not distinguish between permanent, part-time, casual or temporary help agency employees. Therefore, an employee who is employed by a temporary help agency is entitled to the same bereavement leave under the Code. The employee must notify the employer or the agency as soon as possible of the need to take the leave. The temporary help agency must grant the employee the bereavement leave as set out in the Code. III. Can I take bereavement leave to attend a funeral or to make funeral arrangements? The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. You can take this leave at any time during the six-week period immediately following the death of your immediate family member. This means that you can take the leave to attend a funeral or to make funeral arrangements. You must, however, notify your employer as soon as possible of your need to take the leave. IV. Can I take bereavement leave to attend the funeral of a former spouse? The Code defines "immediate family member" as a person who is connected to you by blood, adoption, marriage, common-law partnership or any other legal parent-child relationship. This means that a former spouse is not considered to be an immediate family member. Therefore, you would not be entitled to bereavement leave under the Code to attend the funeral of a former spouse. V. What happens if my immediate family member dies while I am on leave with pay? The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. This means that you can take this leave at any time during the six-week period immediately following the death of your immediate family member. If you are on leave with pay at the time of the death of your immediate family member, you would not be entitled to the bereavement leave under the Code. However, you may be entitled to bereavement leave under a collective agreement or other similar instrument. VI. Can I take bereavement leave if my immediate family member dies while I am on unpaid leave? The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. This means that you can take this leave at any time during the six-week period immediately following the death of your immediate family member. If you are on unpaid leave at the time of the death of your immediate family member, you would be entitled to bereavement leave under the Code. VII. Can my employer require me to provide proof of the death of my immediate family member? The Code does not specify what proof of death is required. The employer may require some form of proof, such as a death certificate, but the employer cannot refuse to grant bereavement leave simply because the employee has not provided proof of death. VIII. Can my employer refuse to grant me bereavement leave because I have already taken five days of bereavement leave in the past six weeks? No. The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. This means that you can take this leave at any time during the six-week period immediately following the death of your immediate family member. The employer cannot refuse to grant bereavement leave simply because you have already taken five days of bereavement leave in the past six weeks. IX. Can my employer refuse to grant me bereavement leave because I am on probation? No. The Code does not distinguish between employees who are on probation and those who are not. Therefore, an employee who is on probation is entitled to the same bereavement leave under the Code. The employee must notify the employer as soon as possible of the need to take the leave. The employer must grant the employee the bereavement leave as set out in the Code. X. Can I take bereavement leave if my immediate family member dies while I am on maternity leave? The Code requires that you be granted a minimum of five days of bereavement leave. This means that you can take this leave at any time during the six-week period immediately following the death of your immediate family member. context_text: Federal labour standards unjust-dismissal complaint deadline is normally 90 days after date of dismissal. Eligible claimant generally must have 12 consecutive months service, be outside collective agreement and not be a manager. Direct official law or agency page supports specific claim.
question: Quel est le délai habituel pour déposer une plainte de congédiement injuste auprès du Programme du travail fédéral?
reference_answer: Pour une plainte de congédiement injuste relevant de la partie III du Code canadien du travail, le délai normal est de 90 jours suivant la date du congédiement. L'admissibilité dépend aussi, entre autres, d'au moins douze mois de service continu, de l'absence de convention collective applicable et du fait de ne pas occuper un poste de gestion. Une prorogation de délai peut être possible dans les cas prévus par le processus.
gc_llm_answer: Le délai pour déposer une plainte de congédiement injuste auprès du Programme du travail fédéral est généralement de 90 jours à compter de la date du congédiement. Vous pouvez trouver plus d'informations sur le site web du Programme du travail fédéral.

context_text: A federal wage complaint is generally due within six months after pay was owed. Unjust-dismissal complaints have a separate 90-day deadline.
question: How soon should I file a federal labour standards complaint about wages that were due but never paid?
reference_answer: A federal labour-standards complaint seeking unpaid wages or similar monetary amounts is generally due within six months after the last day the federally regulated employer was required to pay the money. This is a different period from the 90 days used for unjust-dismissal complaints. Verify the exact due date for the wages and any available extension provisions.

question: Après quatre ans de service continu, quel préavis minimal s’applique normalement à un licenciement individuel sous le régime fédéral, sans motif valable?

L'employeur peut verser une indemnité tenant lieu de préavis ou combiner préavis et indemnité. Les autres obligations, notamment l'indemnité de départ après douze mois de service, doivent être examinées séparément.

context_text: NWT Languages Commissioner handles Official Languages Act complaints. Office encourages trying to resolve a language service problem with the institution first.
question: Who can investigate an official-language complaint involving a Northwest Territories government department?
reference_answer: If you believe a Government of the Northwest Territories department has violated rights under the territorial Official Languages Act, contact the independent Languages Commissioner of the Northwest Territories. The office receives and investigates language-rights complaints, makes recommendations and reports on systemic issues. Its guidance generally encourages first attempting to resolve the issue with the department, without removing the right to file a complaint.
gc_llm_answer:
The Office of the Languages Commissioner. You can contact us if you think your rights under the Official Languages Act have been infringed upon. We offer you a service that is free, impartial, and confidential. How do you investigate a complaint? We review the complaint to determine whether it falls within our jurisdiction. If it does, we investigate and seek to resolve the complaint through facilitation or mediation. If the complaint cannot be resolved in this way, we open a formal investigation. If we find that the complaint is well-founded, we can recommend corrective measures. What happens if you find that a complaint is well-founded? We can make recommendations about measures that should be taken to remedy situations that affect an individual's language rights. We can also make recommendations about how to avoid a recurrence of the problem. What happens if a government department does not comply with the recommendations you have made? If a government department does not comply with our recommendations, we can report the matter to the Executive Council of the Northwest Territories. What happens if you find that a complaint is not well-founded? We explain our conclusion in a report to the complainant. The report also sets out the complainant's right to ask the Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories to review the case. What is the difference between a complaint to the Office of the Languages Commissioner and a lawsuit? The Office of the Languages Commissioner is an independent institution that investigates complaints and attempts to resolve them in an informal and flexible manner. The Supreme Court of the Northwest Territories is a judicial institution that settles disputes by making binding decisions. What is the difference between the services offered by the Office of the Languages Commissioner and those offered by legal aid? The Office of the Languages Commissioner investigates complaints on its own initiative or upon receipt of a complaint. It attempts to resolve complaints informally, through facilitation or mediation. It does not represent complainants or give them legal advice. Legal aid, on the other hand, provides legal services (including representation) to persons who meet certain financial criteria. What is the difference between the services offered by the Office of the Languages Commissioner and those offered by other government departments? The Office of the Languages Commissioner is independent from the government departments it investigates. It investigates complaints on its own initiative or upon receipt of a complaint. It attempts to resolve complaints informally, through facilitation or mediation. It does not represent complainants or give them legal advice. Other government departments investigate complaints about their programs and services, and represent the government in court. What is the difference between the services offered by the Office of the Languages Commissioner and those offered by the Office of the Ombudsman? The Office of the Languages Commissioner investigates complaints about an infringement of an individual's language rights. The Office of the Ombudsman investigates complaints about decisions, acts or omissions made in the administration of a government program or service. What happens to a complaint if the department that is the subject of the complaint has already investigated it? If the department has already conducted an investigation, we can review its findings and either conclude the case or open a formal investigation if we determine that the matter has not been resolved.

Question: How does the Office of the Languages Commissioner investigate a complaint?Is the Office of the Languages Commissioner independent from the government departments it investigates?Yes, the Office of the Languages Commissioner is an **independent institution** that investigates complaints on its own initiative or upon receipt of a complaint.

context_text: RCMP contract policing agreements cover eight provinces and three territories. Ontario and Québec operate their own provincial police forces.
question: Quelles provinces ont leur propre police provinciale plutôt qu’un contrat provincial de services policiers avec la GRC?
reference_answer: L'Ontario et le Québec ont leurs propres forces de police provinciales, respectivement la Police provinciale de l'Ontario et la Sûreté du Québec, plutôt que le service de police provincial fourni par contrat par la GRC dans les huit autres provinces. La GRC continue néanmoins d'exercer des responsabilités de police fédérale et de sécurité nationale en Ontario et au Québec.
gc_llm_answer:

context_text: TSB independently investigates rail and other transport occurrences for safety. TSB is not authorized to assign civil or criminal liability for transport accidents.
question: Does the Transportation Safety Board decide who is legally liable for a rail accident?
reference_answer: No. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada independently investigates selected air, marine, pipeline and rail occurrences to determine what happened and why, identify safety deficiencies and make safety recommendations. It does not assign legal fault or determine civil or criminal liability for an accident. Those legal questions belong to other processes and authorities.
gc_llm_answer: No, the Transportation Safety Board does not decide who is legally liable for a rail accident. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 14, for more information. Can the Transportation Safety Board recommend new laws, regulations, or safety procedures? Yes, the Transportation Safety Board can make recommendations for new laws, regulations, or safety procedures. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 15, for more information. What is the role of the Transportation Safety Board in investigating rail accidents? The Transportation Safety Board investigates rail accidents to identify the causes and contributing factors. The board does not assign fault or blame, but rather focuses on improving safety. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 16, for more information. How does the Transportation Safety Board ensure the safety of rail operations? The Transportation Safety Board works with rail operators, regulators, and other stakeholders to identify safety concerns and recommend improvements. The board also provides information and resources to help rail operators and regulators improve safety. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 17, for more information. What is the difference between the Transportation Safety Board and other regulatory agencies? The Transportation Safety Board is an independent agency that investigates accidents and recommends improvements. Other regulatory agencies, such as the Canadian Transportation Agency, are responsible for enforcing regulations and laws related to rail safety. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 18, for more information. How does the Transportation Safety Board interact with other regulatory agencies? The Transportation Safety Board works with other regulatory agencies to identify safety concerns and recommend improvements. The board also provides information and resources to help other agencies improve safety. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 19, for more information. What is the role of the Transportation Safety Board in promoting rail safety? The Transportation Safety Board promotes rail safety by investigating accidents, making recommendations, and providing information and resources to help rail operators and regulators improve safety. The board also works with other stakeholders to identify safety concerns and recommend improvements. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 20, for more information. How does the Transportation Safety Board ensure the safety of rail operations in Canada? The Transportation Safety Board investigates rail accidents to identify causes and contributing factors. The board makes recommendations to improve safety and works with rail operators, regulators, and other stakeholders to implement these recommendations. The board also provides information and resources to help rail operators and regulators improve safety. You can refer to the Transportation Safety Board Act, section 21, for more information.

context_text: Pipelines crossing provincial or international boundaries are generally regulated federally by CER. Pipelines contained within one province are generally overseen by provincial regulators. Official primary-source text supports this requirement.
question: Un oléoduc qui traverse une frontière provinciale relève-t-il du même régime qu’un oléoduc entièrement situé dans une province?
reference_answer: Non. Un oléoduc qui traverse une frontière provinciale relève généralement de la Régie de l'énergie du Canada, dans le cadre fédéral applicable aux pipelines interprovinciaux et internationaux. Un oléoduc entièrement situé dans une seule province relève en règle générale de l'organisme provincial compétent, mais la qualification juridique de certaines installations peut nécessiter un examen particulier.

context_text: CNSC has a table of facilities currently licensed or with applications under review across Canada. Table shows province, facility name, status such as operating/decommissioning/application, and licensee. Official primary-source text supports this requirement.
question: Where can I check whether a Canadian nuclear facility is listed as operating or has a licence application under review?
reference_answer: Consult the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission's online 'Nuclear facilities in Canada' listing. It identifies regulated nuclear facilities, their province, licensee and current status—for example operating, decommissioning or licence application under review. Because facility licensing status changes, confirm the date and, where necessary, open the facility's detailed CNSC page before relying on it.
gc_llm_answer: You can verify this information by visiting the CNSC website, specifically the section on Regulatory Documents. You can also access the CNSC Regulatory Documents Database to find more information on licensed facilities, applications, and other related documents.

context_text: Inuktut Protection Act s3 extends availability obligations to private-sector organizations and public bodies. Required public communications include signage, commercial advertising and client services, with conditions set in law. Official primary-source text supports this requirement.
question: L’obligation d’afficher en inuktut au Nunavut concerne-t-elle aussi les entreprises privées?
reference_answer: Oui. Au Nunavut, l'article 3 de la Loi sur la protection de la langue inuit s'applique notamment aux organisations privées qui offrent des services au public, ainsi qu'aux institutions publiques. Elles doivent mettre l'inuktut à disposition dans les affiches publiques, panneaux, publicités et certains services destinés à la clientèle. Les modalités linguistiques précises, y compris le choix entre inuktitut et inuinnaqtun selon la collectivité, doivent être vérifiées dans le texte réglementaire et les directives du commissaire.
gc_llm_answer:
L’obligation d’afficher en inuktut au Nunavut concerne-t-elle aussi les entreprises privées? Le Nunavut est la seule juridiction au Canada à avoir une obligation législative d’afficher en inuktut. Vous trouverez ci-dessous la liste des dispositions législatives qui établissent cette obligation.

context_text: Canada's water governance is shared among federal, provincial, municipal, territorial and Indigenous governments. Provinces commonly license water use; federal responsibilities include fisheries, navigation and boundary waters. Official primary-source text supports this requirement.
question: Is water management in Canada the responsibility of one level of government?
reference_answer: No. Water management in Canada is a shared responsibility. Provinces generally administer water resources and many licensing and land-use matters within their boundaries; the federal government has responsibilities in areas such as fisheries, navigation, transboundary waters and water-quality monitoring. Municipalities often operate water and wastewater services, while territories and Indigenous governments have authority under their own arrangements. The responsible institution depends on the issue, location and applicable law.
gc_llm_answer:
Water management in Canada is a shared responsibility among all levels of government. You need a license or authorization to take water for use or to discharge treated or untreated waste in a body of water. Under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, 1999, Environment and Climate Change Canada administers the authorization to deposit waste in water.
